summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 15.0% of firms in Other services (NAICS 81, includes grantmaking and civic organizations) reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 13.7% in the prior period. This is the measured adoption figure for the nonprofit-heavy service sector, not a survey of all nonprofits, and it reflects a short two-week recall window.

Per Candid, donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities, which means many will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter. Per the Center for Effective Philanthropy, its AI-focused reporting examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, though the cited page does not provide specific deployment results. The AI Equity Project describes structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs that bring practical AI tools to public libraries and community spaces, with standardized technical curricula and training assets for underrepresented communities.

Per The World of AI, the catalog of nonprofits and open source foundations contains four individually verified organizations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, an evaluation platform; Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education; the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools. The page notes there are no training compute providers, no standards bodies, and no open-model foundations releasing weights, and the entries do not record funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

Per NTEN, nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled, and users, builders, and funders have a responsibility to ensure the equitable use of technology. The AI Equity Project frames its work around making AI accessible, ethical, and practical, and runs an International AI for Impact Challenge for operational algorithms. Candid's donor-side warning is also a risk: if donors rely on AI tools to filter causes, organizations that are not visible to those tools may lose donor contact.

None of the cited sources reports a return-on-investment figure for nonprofit AI deployments, and none describes a regulatory posture specific to nonprofit AI use. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that adoption is modest but rising in nonprofit-heavy service sectors, donor discovery is shifting toward AI-mediated channels, and equity and training capacity are the constraints the sector's own organizations emphasize.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four individually verified nonprofit and open-source foundation organisations, each with a sourced classification note. It reports that LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a neutral evaluation platform used by the AI community, while Khan Academy is described as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that intersect with AI-generated imagery and 3D content, though their primary missions predate AI. The page notes that the list excludes training compute providers, standards bodies, and open-model foundations, and that the entries confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.
